So while many of us in here might be fans or curious about cyberpunk, I have to wonder: what is cyberpunk to you?

 

Obviously one could point out the books and films and traditional music and subculture fashion trends. But what is it to you personally? How does it effect you personally, and I mean, what about it draws you to it? What about the negative points? I ask this because for me personally, cyberpunk draws me in due to its style, the complicated philosophy of survival within a system looking to make you completely dependent of it while trying to remain "human" and be the independent deviant. The fact that there is no such thing as hero or villain. As both has their pos and flaws.

 

But of course I feel there are some things that are off. For one, I think a lot of people too often associate 1980s style cyberpunk as "canon". While it started then, it doesn't mean our view has to stay there. There's quite a bit of modern cyberpunk I feel is simply mislabeled. EG: Watch_Dogs. While the game may have been a bit of a disappointment, to me this game was pure modern cyberpunk. Why the hell Ubisoft marketed as a "hacking game", I'm not entirely sure. But let me give some examples:

 

  • Aiden is an outlaw who's niether hero nor villain. He is what he is. A survivalist, someone going day to day with a particular goal and trying to reach that goal by any means necessary. Hell, even the karma system is useless because in cyberpunk, KARMA IS USELESS. I wish I could remember his name, but like some Canadian comedian said: "Karma is just Catholic guilt for the hipster generation".

 

  • He's a lot more complex than people give Ubisoft credit for. I mean, no protagonist is just told the truth in any cyberpunk. They have to find it. And when you learn about Aiden and his past, you realize he's not just some poorly written hash character, but rather a stoic individual who not only lost someone he loved dearly, but even a child of war.(Reading certain texts about his past, you see that he was born in Belfast in the 1970s... Yeah, rather violent time there)

 

  • While all the hacks done from the phone seem cool but impossible, many can not be done from a phone, but ever one of those hacks are not only possible... They've been done before in real life. Yeah, even shutting off someone's pacemaker over a wifi/nfc like connection. So forget about predictions of future tech, they're telling you about possibilities you didn't even want to know.

 

I could go on, but this isn't a defense of the game. Rather, I feel that the style of cyberpunk, or at least how many see it, needs to evolve past the 1980s nostalgia, as we're already living in a cyberpunk world now. I thought Watch_Dogs did a great job in evolving it into something beyond the cliche. But I still ask, what are your views?
So what is Cyberpunk to you?

Cyberpunk as a genre is only something I became aware of late last year but it's something I've been interested in ever since I was young, mostly through films, TV and music. Basically I liked all the individual components before I knew how they all fitted together. It's a genre that I'm very interested in with the visual aesthetics but also for the social implications.

I'm interested in not only how humanity is developing technology for the future but how that technology is effecting our day to day lives. Videodrome being the first film I saw that best represents this, but it also shows how its impossible to predict the future. The idea of being consumed by technology was correct but the device that would do it (The TV screen) was wrong. The device that has ended up consuming peoples lives today is a black mirror in our hands or on our desks with a constant stream of updated information most of which is irrelevant and distracting.

I suppose for me cyberpunk represents the constant battle of remaining human while the technology evolves around us. Luckily I feel there will always be those that rebel, hacking/adapting the technology rather than just consuming and being controlled by it. I'm drawn to the technology that can free us rather than just keep us controlled or distracted.
I have a lot on common with you in that I only became aware of cyberpunk as genre very recently, but I have been in love with the aesthetics of it my entire life.

Advent of the internet in every household in the 90s kind of killed it in the sense, and as the world moved into post-cyberpunk territory, so did the novels. Then again, I consider the documentation of the trials of folks like Kevin Mitnick, Snowden, even Kim Dotcom to be as cyberpunk as anything that has come out since Snow Crash. Couple that with all that is being pushed forward by the likes of DARPA, Academi formerly known as Blackwater, Google, the entire "too big to fail" economic bubble burst that was built on advanced algorithms in trading markets, the rise of vocaloids, holographic celebrity appearances, ... as Gibson said "that truth-is-stranger-than-fiction factor keeps getting jacked up on us on a fairly regular, maybe even exponential, basis. I think that's something peculiar to our time." I have a pocket, online computer, at all times, that can be set up to create adhoc communications networks, that has been used to "sniff" unencrypted passwords in the past. That is not fiction.

And like all things, a good dose of retro-futurism, mixed with nostalgia ensures that some level lives on currently as 80s neon, gritty economic collapse with technological advances. Other things, you look at say, the new Mirror's Edge trailer, and start deconstructing just how many different aspects actually fit with the same dystopia in the Sprawl, just with a modern aesthetic. EDIT: Forgot three words.

My entry into Cyberpunk was through various anime, movies, and games like Ghost in the Shell, Gundam, Serial Experiments, The Matrix, Starwars, Metal Gear, Bioschock, Fallout, Psycho-Pass, and even Full Metal Alchemist to some extent before I'd known that it was even a genre. Books like Brave new world, Neuromancer, 1984, Feed, Daemon, and certain types of conspiracy literature are also other obvious gateway novels even though I haven't read all of these. Overall, I also think cyberpunk does well at depicting how different characters find creative ways of navigating through decaying societeis as technology advances faster. Something else I appreciate about Cyberpunk is that moral ambiguity within this genre reflects how fragmented the human condition, or collective psyche, can become from traumas caused through technologies created by autocratic thought patterns.
